source.version: Journal article in Journal of Inclusive Methodology and Technology in Learning and Teaching, Anno 6 n. 1 (2026), copyright 2026 (p. 1). No publication-day date is printed in the document; the search record and local filenames use 2025.
source.title_on_document: Exploring the Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Creative Thinking Processes: results from a preliminary study.

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is referenced in the PDF. Results are in the main text, pp. 6?8; references occupy pp. 11?12.

paper_design_summary: University students recruited during regular coursework were reportedly randomly assigned to use generative AI on two analytical reading questions or to complete the activity without digital tools, although the article labels the design quasi-experimental (pp. 3?4, Sections 2.1?2.2). Both groups subsequently wrote a social-media post assessed with a creative-production rubric; AI permission was restricted to the preceding analytical questions, so the post comparison is coded after_ai (pp. 3?6, Sections 2.1?2.3). The creative-performance analysis includes 56 students, 28 per arm; A.S.K. creative potential and self-reported AI familiarity are also described and correlated with post performance (p. 6, Table 1; pp. 7?8, Sections 3.3?3.5).

studies.label: Creative social-media post after AI-assisted versus unaided text analysis

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual university students were assigned to an experimental group permitted to use AI for the first two Analysis/Evaluation questions or a control group completing the entire activity without digital support. The subsequent Creation question was common to both groups. The paper explicitly states random assignment despite using the label quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: The sample, composed of university students, was randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 2.1 Research Design; conflicting quasi-experimental terminology also appears in p. 1 Abstract and pp. 9?10, Section 5 Limitations.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is reported in the PDF (pp. 1?12).

arms.name: Group A ? with AI
arms.description: Generative AI permitted for the two analytical questions preceding creative production; subsequently completed the common social-media post task. AI use was limited to the first two questions by the stated protocol (p. 3, Section 2.1). Analyzed arm count is from p. 6, Table 1.

arms.name: Group B ? without digital tools
arms.description: Completed the whole activity, including the analytical questions and creative post, without any digital support (p. 3, Section 2.1). Analyzed arm count is from p. 6, Table 1.

participants.exclusions: Exclusions and attrition are not reported. The single Management Engineering master?s student was explicitly retained in the analyses (p. 4, Section 2.2). Sample and analysis counts are reported, but no separate count at random assignment is given.
participants.who: Convenience sample of university students recruited during regular coursework, predominantly in economics-related programs. Although the sample is described as undergraduate, the paper explicitly includes one master?s student in Management Engineering (p. 4, Section 2.2).
participants.quote: The sample consisted of 56 undergraduate students
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.2 Sample; p. 6, Table 1 reports 28 analyzed students in each arm.

ai_tool.how_used: Unspecified generative AI tools were permitted to support responses to two Analysis/Evaluation questions about a disciplinary reading before the creative post was produced (p. 3, Section 2.1; p. 1, Abstract). Role is coded other for analytical reading support. The provider, model, interface, prompts, usage amount, and compliance checks are not reported. Interaction strategies were not directly observed or standardized (p. 9, Section 4).

task.description: Read Matteo Minelli?s ?Tribal Economy: When Not Doing Becomes Abundance,? answer the preceding analytical questions, and create a post for Instagram, X/Twitter, or Facebook of up to 800 characters, including a title/slogan and an original reworking of abundance and not doing in contemporary society (pp. 3?5, Sections 2.1 and 2.3).

outcomes.name: Total_Create creative-production rubric total
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An analytic rubric assessed the produced social-media post on four indicators: conceptual re-elaboration; originality and synthesis of the message; thematic relevance; and linguistic appropriateness and communicative tone. Each indicator was scored 0?3, with a maximum total of 12 points (pp. 5?6, Section 2.3). Only the total is reported by AI condition (p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2); indicator-specific results are not reported. The paper does not identify who or what applied the rubric, the number or expertise of assessors, blinding, or reliability, so measure is null rather than assuming a rater class. The outcome is produced after the phase in which AI use was permitted (p. 3, Section 2.1).
outcomes.delay: The creative post follows the analytical questions in the same activity; no elapsed time or later-session delay is stated (pp. 3?4, Section 2.1).

contrasts.reported: Group A ? with AI: N = 28, Mean = 8.21, Std. Dev. = 1.97; Group B ? without digital tools: N = 28, Mean = 7.64, Std. Dev. = 1.94. The text reports +0.57 points, p = .31, and Cohen?s d = 0.26. No standard error, confidence interval, test statistic, or degrees of freedom are reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2 Creative Performance Results; interpretation continues on p. 7.

company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; full PDF, pp. 1?12.

eligibility.reason: Section 2.1 explicitly states individual random assignment to AI access versus no digital support (p. 3), despite the paper?s inconsistent quasi-experimental label. The analyzed sample comprises 56 people, with 28 per arm (p. 4, Section 2.2; p. 6, Table 1). A rubric scores the creative post itself, including originality, rather than self-reported creativity (pp. 5?6, Section 2.3). The eligible question is after_ai: permission to use AI was limited to the analytical questions preceding the common creative task (pp. 1 and 3?4). Field RCT is the closest setting category because recruitment occurred during regular university coursework (p. 4); the precise administration setting is not fully described.

one_line_finding: After AI-assisted analysis, the subsequent creative-post score was 8.21 (SD 1.97; n = 28) versus 7.64 (SD 1.94; n = 28) without digital support, with no statistically clear difference (p = .31; reported Cohen?s d = 0.26; p. 6, Table 1 and Section 3.2).
open_questions: How was random assignment implemented, and why does the paper repeatedly call the design quasi-experimental despite explicitly stating random assignment (p. 3, Section 2.1; pp. 9?10, Section 5)?

Was the activity conducted as ordinary coursework or as a separate research session? Recruitment during coursework and online questionnaire collection are reported, but the precise setting is not (p. 4, Sections 2.2?2.3); field_rct is the closest supported setting code.

Which AI tool/model was used, and how was the restriction of AI use to the analytical phase enforced? The timing code follows the stated protocol; access logs or a withdrawal/compliance procedure are not reported (p. 3, Section 2.1).
Who or what scored the creative rubric, and were assessors blinded or reliability assessed? The scoring process is unspecified, preventing a confirmed measure category (pp. 5?6, Section 2.3).

When was the A.S.K. test administered relative to AI exposure, and how should its internally inconsistent gender counts be interpreted? Table 2 prints 20 male and 15 female students in the average band but a total of 37; no explanation is given (p. 7, Table 2).
notes: Screened the entire 12-page PDF and all 365 lines of its markdown conversion. Tables and results were inspected before methods; the PDF contains two results tables and no reported outcome figures or appended supplement. Outcome inventory: (1) Total_Create creative-post total, the only output score compared by AI assignment (p. 6, Table 1); its four rubric components are defined but not reported separately (pp. 5?6). (2) A.S.K. standardized creative-potential scores, based on hypothesis generation, category creation, conditional structure, and sentence invention, are reported as performance bands by gender, not by AI assignment; administration timing and any AI contrast are unstated, so this is documented here rather than counted as an outcome answering the three atlas questions (p. 5, Section 2.3; p. 7, Table 2). Table 2 prints total below-average n = 9 (16.07%), average n = 37 (66.07%), and above-average n = 10 (17.86%); its gender counts contain an inconsistency noted in open_questions. (3) DIGCOMP-based AI familiarity is self-reported, not scored on creative output, and is therefore not an eligible outcome (pp. 5?6, Sections 2.3 and 3.1). The same creative-post total is correlated with overall AI familiarity (r = .46, p < .001), Digital content creation (r = .51, p < .001), Problem solving (r = .48, p < .001), Information and data literacy (r = .34, p < .01), Communication and collaboration (r = .31, p < .01), and Safety (r = .29, p < .05), all on p. 8, Section 3.4; the correlation with A.S.K. creative potential is r = .42, p < .01 (p. 8, Section 3.5). These correlations are not separate outcomes or randomized contrasts. No comprehension-question accuracy results or across-person diversity measures are reported. Counts at randomization are left null because only sample and analysis counts are given. The reported effect size is transcribed without recomputation. No participant reuse, data repository, or code repository is stated in the PDF. The code field_rct follows the reported random assignment and coursework recruitment rather than the unverified search-record design guess; the uncertain setting and conflicting design labels remain explicit.
